result: Refractive index mismatches between media and sample cause spherical aberrations that limit penetration depth and resolution in light microscopy, with effects increasing with specimen complexity and thickness.
evaluation: Claims C1, C5, and C6 establish well-known optical principles supported by appropriate citations (Richardson and Lichtman, 2015). These claims provide the foundational rationale for the study and are consistent with established knowledge in microscopy.

result: Existing optical clearing techniques can render tissues transparent by equilibrating refractive index heterogeneity but are limited to fixed specimens due to harsh mounting conditions and/or toxic chemicals.
evaluation: Claims C2, C11, and C12 accurately describe the state of the field with appropriate citations (Chung et al., 2013; Hama et al., 2015; Richardson and Lichtman, 2015). This establishes the gap that the current work addresses.

result: Alternative microscopy approaches including 2-photon microscopy and adaptive optics have limitations: 2-photon microscopy cannot alleviate spherical aberrations, while adaptive optics requires reduced acquisition rates and intense excitation light.
evaluation: Claims C7-C10 accurately characterize existing technologies with appropriate citations (Helmchen and Denk, 2005; Booth, 2014; Richardson and Lichtman, 2015). These claims establish the context for why a new approach is needed.

result: Iodixanol, originally developed as an X-ray contrast agent and used in density gradients, is commercially available as OptiPrep™, is optically clear, and displays a high refractive index of 1.429 at 60% concentration, comparable to fixed tissue clearing solutions.
evaluation: Claims C13-C21 provide well-documented background on Iodixanol with appropriate citations (Albrechtsson et al., 1992; Bettinger et al., 2002; Richardson and Lichtman, 2015; Ku et al., 2016). The measured RI value (C17) is supported by Figure 1a data.

result: Iodixanol is highly water-soluble and can be diluted to linearly tune refractive index between 1.333-1.429, with minimal effect from different aqueous media (water, PBS, culture media) at a given concentration.
evaluation: Claims C22-C24 are directly supported by experimental data in Figure 1a showing linear relationships (r² > 0.999) with technical triplicates. The linearity and minimal medium effects are clearly demonstrated.

result: The temperature-dependent change in refractive index of Iodixanol solutions is minimal within physiologically relevant temperature ranges, allowing use of the same medium at multiple temperatures.
evaluation: Claims C25-C26 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1b. The minimal temperature dependence is demonstrated empirically, and the inference about multi-temperature use (C26) is reasonable given the data.

result: Iodixanol is compatible with agarose embedding protocols: agarose polymerization is not prevented at any Iodixanol concentration, and agarose concentrations used for specimen immobilization do not significantly affect refractive index.
evaluation: Claims C27-C29 are supported by experimental data in Figure 1c. The compatibility with agarose is important for practical applications and is well-demonstrated with appropriate controls.

result: Iodixanol solutions show no significant autofluorescence at commonly used excitation wavelengths (405, 488, 560, 640 nm) compared to PBS and fluorescent bead controls.
evaluation: Claim C30 is supported by spectral emission data in Figure 1d and Figure 1—figure supplement 1. The comparison with appropriate negative (PBS) and positive (beads) controls strengthens this conclusion.

result: Iodixanol solutions have no significant pH buffering capacity within the physiologically relevant pH range (pH 4-9) and are only slightly more acidic than water.
evaluation: Claims C31-C32 are supported by pH titration data in Figure 1e with appropriate comparison to PBS as a buffering control. This is important for biological compatibility.

result: 60% Iodixanol stock solution has an osmolality of 212±2 mmol/kg (below typical vertebrate cell culture media at 290-300 mmol/kg), with linear increase across dilutions, allowing osmolality adjustment by offsetting with reduced salt concentration.
evaluation: Claims C33-C37 are supported by osmolality measurements in Figure 1f with technical triplicates and linear regression (r² > 0.981). The inference about salt compensation (C37) is reasonable given the linear relationship. Citation to Ke et al., 2013 appropriately contextualizes the importance.

result: Tuning the refractive index of bead solutions to match silicone immersion oil (RI=1.40) greatly improved both lateral and axial image resolution compared to aqueous media (RI=1.33), demonstrating that Iodixanol's physicochemical properties are ideally suitable for RI tuning of live imaging media.
evaluation: Claims C38-C39 are supported by point spread function measurements in Figure 1g,h and Supplementary file 1. The proof-of-principle demonstration with fluorescent beads provides strong evidence for the optical benefits of RI matching.

result: Iodixanol shows no concentration-dependent effects on HeLa cell proliferation or death up to 3 days at concentrations up to 30% (RI=1.380), which exceeds the optimal concentration needed for these cells.
evaluation: Claims C40-C41 are supported by quantitative data in Figure 2a and Figure 2—figure supplement 1. Statistical analysis (p>0.05, one-way ANOVA) and testing above optimal concentration strengthen the toxicity assessment. However, only one cell line was tested.

result: Zebrafish embryos exposed to Iodixanol (20% w/v) for 3 days showed normal motility, muscle contractions, pigmentation, survival rates, and head-to-tail length, indicating no overt effects on development or survival.
evaluation: Claims C42-C44 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2b with appropriate sample size (N=30) and statistical analysis (p>0.05, paired t-test). Multiple developmental parameters were assessed, strengthening the conclusion.

result: Planarians exposed to 50% w/v Iodixanol for 3 weeks remained healthy, regenerated morphologically normal heads, and restored normal body plan proportions (length/width ratio, projected area) indistinguishably from controls.
evaluation: Claims C45-C46 are supported by experimental data in Figure 2c with quantitative morphometric analysis and statistical testing (p>0.05, paired t-test). The 3-week exposure period is particularly impressive for demonstrating long-term compatibility.

result: Iodixanol supplementation minimally impacts survival and growth of cell cultures, embryonic development, and tissue turnover/regeneration in intact animals, alleviating toxicity concerns.
evaluation: Claim C47 is a reasonable synthesis of the toxicity data from C40-C46 across multiple model systems. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective evidence, though testing in additional cell types and organisms would strengthen generalizability.

result: Silicone oil immersion objectives (RI=1.406) closely match typical live specimens and have afforded substantial improvements in live imaging quality.
evaluation: Claims C48-C49 establish context with appropriate citation (York et al., 2012). This provides the reference point for evaluating Iodixanol's performance.

result: In primary zebrafish cell clusters, nuclear chromatin structure was indiscernible in cells behind the first layer in unsupplemented media, but tuning media RI to 1.362 reduced resolution degradation in deeper cells.
evaluation: Claims C50-C51 are supported by imaging data in Figure 3a and Figure 3—figure supplement 1. The intensity profiles quantitatively demonstrate preservation of chromatin fine structure with RI matching.

result: Human cerebral organoids appear opaque due to neuronal tissue optical density, limiting conventional single photon microscopy to ~20 µm depth, but Iodixanol supplementation (RI=1.363) doubled penetration depth to ~40 µm through improved signal-to-noise ratios.
evaluation: Claims C52-C55 are supported by experimental data in Figure 3b with appropriate citation (Lancaster and Knoblich, 2014). The doubling of penetration depth is clearly demonstrated, though the improvement is modest in absolute terms.

result: In zebrafish embryos, RI tuning to 1.363 improved lateral resolution from 918±50 nm to 792±28 nm at 150 µm depth, with benefits increasing with distance from coverslip as expected from spherical aberration theory, enabling nuclear segmentation up to 300 µm depth.
evaluation: Claims C56-C61 are well-supported by quantitative PSF measurements in Figure 4a and nuclear segmentation data in Figure 4—figure supplement 1. The depth-dependent improvement is consistent with optical theory (C59) and demonstrates substantial practical benefit.

result: Live imaging of planarian regeneration has been impossible because even unpigmented species are highly opaque, restricting imaging to the epithelium, but RI tuning to 1.412 partially compensated opacity and significantly improved signal detection in deeper layers, bringing live regeneration imaging within reach.
evaluation: Claims C62-C66 are supported by imaging data in Figure 4b with appropriate citation (Liu et al., 2013). The improvement in deeper tissue imaging is demonstrated, though the claim about bringing regeneration imaging 'within reach' (C66) is somewhat speculative without actual regeneration time-lapse data.

result: Iodixanol supplementation is a simple, versatile, and effective method for RI tuning that provides substantial improvements in imaging depth (planaria, zebrafish, organoids) and spatial resolution (cell cultures), enabling optical axis alignment in live specimens previously only possible in fixed samples.
evaluation: Claims C67-C70 represent appropriate synthesis of the imaging results across multiple model systems. The conclusion is well-supported by the collective experimental evidence, though 'ideally suitable' may be somewhat overstated.

result: Iodixanol cannot correct for refractive index differences within specimens (between cells or organelles), which likely causes opacity in planarians and organoids, and cannot achieve in-toto RI matching of fixed tissue protocols, but nevertheless demonstrates substantial imaging improvements in opaque specimens.
evaluation: Claims C71-C74 appropriately acknowledge limitations of the method. The speculation about internal RI differences causing opacity (C72) is reasonable but not directly tested. The acknowledgment of limitations compared to fixed tissue methods (C73) is honest and appropriate.

result: Refractive index tuning by Iodixanol supplementation represents a broadly useful addition to the toolkit of live-imaging applications from cells to tissues and organisms.
evaluation: Claim C75 is a reasonable concluding statement supported by the breadth of applications demonstrated (cells, organoids, embryos, adult organisms). The expectation of broad utility is justified by the experimental evidence, though marked as speculation.

result: Iodixanol is a non-toxic medium supplement that allows refractive index matching in live specimens and substantially improves image quality in live-imaged primary cell cultures, planarians, zebrafish, and human cerebral organoids.
evaluation: Claims C3-C4 represent the main findings of the paper and are well-supported by the comprehensive toxicity data (Figure 2) and imaging improvements across multiple model systems (Figures 3-4). This is the central contribution of the work.

result: Methodological details including measurement conditions, instrumentation, cell line authentication, animal husbandry, and sample preparation protocols are documented.
evaluation: Claims C76-C88 provide essential methodological information with appropriate detail and citations. Cell line authentication (C81-C82) and mycoplasma testing (C83) are particularly important quality control measures. Methods appear reproducible.
